qs.q: Which of the following viral haemorrhagic fevers has a widely available live attenuated vaccine providing protection for up to 30-35 years?
qs.e: Yellow fever has a live attenuated single-dose vaccine that confers immunity in 1 week in 95% of people and protects for 30-35 years. Vaccines for Dengue and Rift Valley fever are still under trial or unavailable.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Live attenuated vaccines use weakened organisms that can replicate, inducing strong, long‑lasting immunity but pose risks in immunocompromised patients. They are key in many childhood schedules, yet contraindicated in pregnancy and primary immunodeficiencies.

sections.p: Live attenuated vaccines contain organisms that have been weakened so they can replicate only briefly, mimicking natural infection and stimulating robust cellular and humoral responses.
The pathogen is genetically or chemically altered to reduce virulence while preserving immunogenic antigens. Replication is limited to a few cycles.
b: Replicates in host but not enough to cause disease
Preserves key surface proteins for immune recognition

sections.p: After administration, the attenuated organism infects mucosal or skin sites, replicates locally, and is cleared by the immune system. No onward transmission occurs.
In healthy hosts, the vaccine may cause mild, self‑limited symptoms (e.g., nasal congestion with LAIV). In immunocompromised hosts, it can lead to full‑blown disease.
b: Severe disease in immunodeficient or pregnant

sections.p: Clinical recognition of vaccine‑related symptoms is usually sufficient. If severe disease is suspected, PCR or viral culture confirms the attenuated strain.
Treat underlying disease with supportive care. Antivirals (acyclovir/valacyclovir) are used if severe disease occurs. Prevention relies on contraindication in high‑risk groups.
Remember that live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in primary immunodeficiency, pregnancy, and severe immunosuppression. They provide lifelong immunity after a single dose in many cases.
Inactivated vaccines (cannot replicate) and subunit vaccines (only antigens).
PCR may detect vaccine RNA long after inoculation, potentially confusing with wild‑type infection. Clinical context is essential.

faq.q: Why are live attenuated vaccines contraindicated in pregnancy?
faq.a: The weakened pathogen can cross the placenta and cause fetal infection, as seen with rubella vaccine.

faq.q: Can a live attenuated vaccine revert to a virulent form?
faq.a: Rarely; genetic stability is engineered, but theoretical risk exists, especially in immunocompromised hosts.

faq.q: What is the advantage of a single‑dose live attenuated vaccine?
faq.a: It induces long‑lasting immunity with minimal exposure, improving compliance and reducing cost.
